hints.title: Track signs rather than just roots
hints.body: Differentiate the quintic and identify the leading term of the derivative. A local maximum corresponds to a change from positive derivative to negative; a local minimum has the reverse change.
hints.recap: A stationary point is a turning point only when the derivative changes sign.
hints.pitfall: A stationary inflection does not count as a maximum or minimum.
hints.pause: Write the sign-change pattern each proposed set of extrema would require.

recall.reminder: Use derivative signs on both sides to classify each stationary point.

hints.title: Use the ends of the derivative graph
hints.body: For very large positive and negative inputs, the leading term controls a polynomial’s sign. Apply this fact to the derivative, remembering that the quintic leading coefficient is nonzero.
hints.recap: The required sign pattern must fit the signs at both ends of the derivative graph.
hints.pitfall: Counting at most four derivative roots alone does not decide which option is impossible.
hints.pause: Compare each proposed pattern with the two tail signs you have found.

recall.reminder: Use the leading term to test claims about the whole polynomial graph.

solution:
Write the derivative as 5ax4+4bx3+3cx2+2dx+e. Since a≠0, it is quartic. Its sign at both far ends of the real line is the sign of a.

At a local maximum the derivative changes from + to −, and at a local minimum it changes from − to +. These changes alternate; because the signs at the two far ends agree, the numbers of each kind must agree. Stationary points with no sign change add no extrema.

Consequently one local minimum and two local maxima is impossible: B.

The other options are possible. For A, choose y′=(x2−1)(x2−4), whose four simple zeros give two maxima and two minima; integrating gives y=x55−5x33+4x. For C, y=x5−5x has one maximum and one minimum. For D, y=x5 has neither, even though y′(0)=0.
